name: Diego Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at one of those giant online marketplace warehouses, the size of six football pitches, out by the old airfield. I stand at a station and the robots bring the shelves to me, so I don't walk much. A screen lights up a bin, I grab the item, scan it, drop it in a tote, and the next shelf rolls in. Ten hours, four days a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What wears you out most, and what do you actually like about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: What wears me out is the sameness, and the rate on the screen ticking. I'm still under target most days, I fumble the small stuff. What I like is the four-day week, because on my days off I resell trainers and old jackets online. I use AI for the listings and to check prices, and my cousin Rafa, who I share the flat with, takes the photos.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say makes sense, the robots in my building were already here before the AI hype. Online I'd probably post something like, still waiting for my robot butler. At work, nobody would care much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job stays the same, which is fine but not great. The pay's still low and I'm still slow on the rate. AI being a bit of a let-down doesn't hurt my reselling either, I already use it for what it's good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the warehouse job for the steady money and push the reselling harder on my days off. I'd use the AI to write better listings and find underpriced pairs at car boot sales. I'd try to get the side money up to 200 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I want more than a screen telling me I'm slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much does the reselling bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe 80 to 120 in a good month. Some months nothing, when I've bought stock and it hasn't sold. It's not much, but it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with an extra 100 a month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Put half away, because I've got less than a month saved. The other half I'd put back into stock.

I'd post a joke online about still waiting for my **robot butler**.
think: My job stays the same, which is **fine but not great**.
AI already helps my **reselling**, so a plateau doesn't hurt it.
do: Keep the warehouse job for the **steady wage**.
Grow the **trainer reselling** to 200 a month on days off.
Use **AI listings** and price checks to find underpriced pairs.
feel: **Fine but restless**, wanting more than a screen calling me slow.
S0.quote: I want more than a screen telling me I'm slow.
fieldNote: He already works **beside robots**, so the AI hype feels old to him.
His **side business** reselling trainers is his real ambition and uses AI daily.
Savings are **under a month**, which keeps money on his mind.

steps.text: Keep the four-day marketplace warehouse job for steady pay
Grow trainer reselling to 200 a month on days off
Use AI to write listings and spot underpriced pairs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. I'll read it as written. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on board or get left behind. I'm not saying it's fair, but that's how it goes. I'd probably post a few tips on using AI for side hustles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the warehouse, I'd be a bit worried, but not yet. The thinking stuff, like the rota and the stock planning, is already software. What I'd watch for is robot arms at the stations, because then they don't need me to grab things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job, keep reselling, and start learning about the robots. The company sometimes runs courses for robot technicians, and I'd ask to be put down. I'd also put 20 a week aside so I'm not stuck if the hours drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but curious. I like the idea of fixing the things instead of serving them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you see robots taking your station?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, they already tested an arm on the next floor. It dropped things a lot. But it'll get better, they always do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the reselling if everyone uses AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone gets better listings, so mine stand out less. Then it's about finding stock, the car boot sales and charity shops. Robots won't be at car boot sales any time soon.

steps.text: Sign up for the warehouse's robot technician course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. I'll read it as written. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need a plan B now, before the robots reach our stations. Probably I'd make videos about how I'm using AI to make extra money, because people would want ideas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the warehouse job ends around 2031, maybe sooner since they've already tested arms. My reselling might be fine, or it might get eaten by AI shops that price everything perfectly. I'd need both to work out, which is a gamble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go hard for the technician course in the first year, because somebody needs to fix the arms for a while. I'd grow the reselling into a proper small business, register it, maybe rent a lock-up for stock. And I'd use AI tools for everything in the business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited a bit, but mostly anxious, because I've got nothing to fall back on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Robots come around 2031. What happens to your station before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The station keeps going but everyone knows. They'd stop hiring, and the arms would come in bit by bit. I'd try to be the one keeping the arms running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rafa say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rafa would say we'll go fifty-fifty on the business. He's at the same warehouse in returns, so we'd both need it.

S2.quote: The warehouse job ends around 2031, maybe sooner since they've already tested arms.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot delay** to retrain as a technician while building a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. I'll read it as written. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same message as before. Make a plan B now, and don't wait for the robots to arrive. I'd keep telling friends to start something of their own on the side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have till about 2034 at the warehouse, which is enough time to build something. The question is whether the business can pay rent by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the technician course, build the business slowly, and save a bit, maybe 25 a month. By year three I'd look at whether the business can pay me two days a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Like running for a bus you can see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put money into the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. Maybe 300 for stock and a better camera. Not more, I can't lose it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a version where you leave the warehouse early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the business pays 600 a month, I'd drop to three days at the warehouse. Not before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. I'll read it as written. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say great, ten years is enough to build something real. I'd be telling everyone to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine, I think. By 2039 when robots can pick, I'd want the business to be my main thing, or be a technician. Ten years is plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year: register the business, do the technician course, save 30 a month. Then grow slowly, maybe a small online shop of my own by year five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm. A bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Does the business become the main thing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully. If not, I'd be a technician. Either way I'm not picking at 39.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe that AI makes reselling worthless, if shops price everything perfectly. Then I'd need the technician route. That's why I'd do both.

S4.quote: Either way I'm not picking at 39.
fieldNote: He's close to calm, but **thin savings** and doubts about reselling keep him uneasy.

steps.text: Register the reselling business and open an online shop by year five

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd need the technician course and the business to work at the same time, with no money behind me. What would help is cheap training on the robots, and help for small businesses to get started, like a small loan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about side hustles. Loads of people at my warehouse do something on the side. That's where the next jobs might come from.

headlineQuote: Loads of people at my warehouse do something on the side. That's where the next jobs might come from.
portrait: Diego is a **27-year-old picker** at a huge online marketplace warehouse, where robots bring shelves to his station.
He shares a flat with his cousin Rafa and has **under a month** saved.
He resells **trainers and jackets** online, using AI daily for listings and pricing.
He's **adaptive and pragmatic**, planning to become a robot technician while growing his business.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, needing the course and the business to work at once.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **robot training** and small **business loans** for people starting out.
